title: Constructing Doppelgängers of Greedy Geometric Spanners in Practice
abstract:
Greedy geometric spanners are considered to be the gold standard for their near-optimal guarantees in terms of sparsity and total weight. However, their inefficient construction poses significant challenges for large-scale geometric networks, especially for low values of stretch factors (< 2). We present Θ-Greedy, a simple and practical parallel algorithm engineered for constructing doppelgängers of greedy geometric spanners that empirically resemble the greedy spanners in key structural and performance metrics, including average degree, degree, and lightness. Unlike approximate greedy spanners, doppelgängers of greedy spanners are almost indistinguishable from the actual greedy spanners in practice.
In our experiments, Θ-Greedy consistently produced greedy spanner doppelgängers across a broad range of synthetic and real-world datasets, offering the first practical alternative to the computationally intensive greedy spanners. Θ-Greedy can construct a 1.1-spanner on a 128K-element uniformly distributed point set in well under 5 minutes. In contrast, Bucketing, the most practical greedy spanner algorithm, takes around 3 hours. For million-sized point sets, Θ-Greedy can run to completion in a few hours, making it much faster than Bucketing, which takes days to finish. In extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, Θ-Greedy delivered speedups of up to 147x over Bucketing while preserving greedy-like sparsity and weight. 
For broader uses of the algorithm and reproducibility, we share our engineered C++ code.

      Abstract
Greedy geometric spanners are considered to be the gold standard for their near-optimal guarantees in
terms of sparsity and total weight. However, their inefficient construction poses significant challenges
for large-scale geometric networks, especially for low values of stretch factors (< 2). We present
Θ-Greedy, a simple and practical parallel algorithm engineered for constructing doppelgängers
of greedy geometric spanners that empirically resemble the greedy spanners in key structural and
performance metrics, including average degree, degree, and lightness. Unlike approximate greedy
spanners, doppelgängers of greedy spanners are almost indistinguishable from the actual greedy
spanners in practice.
     In our experiments, Θ-Greedy consistently produced greedy spanner doppelgängers across
a broad range of synthetic and real-world datasets, offering the first practical alternative to the
computationally intensive greedy spanners. Θ-Greedy can construct a 1.1-spanner on a 128K-
element uniformly distributed point set in well under 5 minutes. In contrast, Bucketing, the most
practical greedy spanner algorithm, takes around 3 hours. For million-sized point sets, Θ-Greedy
can run to completion in a few hours, making it much faster than Bucketing, which takes days to
finish. In extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, Θ-Greedy delivered speedups
of up to 147x over Bucketing while preserving greedy-like sparsity and weight.
     For broader uses of the algorithm and reproducibility, we share our engineered C++ code.

 1      Introduction
A geometric spanner on a set of points P in L2 metric is a sparse subgraph of the complete
Euclidean graph on P that approximately preserves pairwise distances among all point pairs
in P . Formally, given a set of n points P ⊂ Rd and a stretch factor t ≥ 1, a geometric graph
H := (P, E) is a t-spanner if, for all u, v ∈ P , the shortest-path distance in H, denoted
by δH (u, v), satisfies δH (u, v) ≤ t · |uv|, where |uv| denotes the Euclidean distance between
u, v. A t-spanner is also a t′ -spanner, for all t′ ≥ t. A t-path exists between two points in a
geometric graph H if δH (u, v) ≤ t · |uv|. Therefore, H is a t-spanner if for every point pair in
P , a t-path exists in H. The average degree of H is defined as 2|E|/|n|, and its lightness is
the ratio of the weight of H to the weight of a Euclidean minimum spanning tree of P . For a
fixed value of t, lower average   degree and lightness are better. The complete Euclidean graph
is a 1-spanner with n2 = Θ(n2 ) edges, rendering it impractical for large-scale applications.
                         

So, the study of geometric spanners focuses on designing algorithms that construct sparse
t-spanners, ideally with O(n) edges, while maintaining desirable geometric and algorithmic
properties; see [13, 28, 34] for a comprehensive overview. Spanners play a central role in

       computational geometry and the design of geometric networks. They are widely used in
       applications such as wireless networks, motion planning, and approximation algorithms,
       where maintaining low stretch with minimal edge cost is essential [5, 18, 24, 27, 30, 31].
           Introduced by Althöfer et al. [4] and also by Chandra et al. [16] more than 30 years ago,
       the greedy spanner is a cornerstone in the study of geometric spanner networks, offering near-
       optimal guarantees in terms of sparsity and weight (also lightness) [10, 20, 21, 26, 32]. The
       greedy spanner is naively constructed by processing all pairs of points in order of increasing
       Euclidean distance and adding an edge between each pair (u, v) if the current shortest path
       between them exceeds t · |uv|, where t ≥ 1 is the desired stretch factor. The algorithm,
       known as Path-Greedy in the literature, is a generalization of the textbook Kruskal’s
       algorithm. Refer to Figure 1 for greedy spanner examples. A straightforward implementation
       of Path-Greedy runs in O(n3 log n) time since there are n2 point pairs, and for every pair,
       computation of a shortest path takes O(n log n) time, as greedy spanners are linear-sized
       spanners. It also uses Θ(n2 ) space to store and sort all point pairs, making it impractical
       for large point sets. A variant (still using Θ(n2 ) extra space), named FG-Greedy, was
       introduced by Farshi and Gudmundsson [22], to speed up the algorithm by reducing the
       number of shortest-path calls. The idea was to memorize the shortest-path lengths obtained
       by previous single-source shortest-path calls using a matrix, allowing future calls to be avoided
       using simple lookups. Surprisingly, it was shown in [11] that FG-Greedy runs in O(n3 log n)
       time, although in experiments, it was found to be faster than Path-Greedy; refer to [22].
       Das and Narasimhan made the first attempt to approximate greedy spanners in [19], wherein
       they designed the Approximate-Greedy algorithm that runs in O(n log2 n) time. See
       Table 1. Despite being theoretically novel, experimental studies [22, 32] on spanners found
       that Approximate-Greedy places substantially more edges compared to actual greedy
       spanners, rendering them impractical for real-world applications. Bose et al. [12] designed
       an O(n2 log n)-time algorithm to construct exact greedy spanners using Θ(n2 ) space, an
       improvement over Path-Greedy. To see how frustrating quadratic space algorithms are

       sets. The parameter δ controls the trade-off between construction time and similarity to
       the Path-Greedy spanner; setting δ = t yields an identical spanner. However, the space
       complexity is quadratic, making it impractical for large point sets. Therefore, we decided
       not to include it in our experiments.
           Shariful et al. [32] recently observed that Bucketing is slow for large values of n.
       For instance, when n = 106 , t = 1.1, and the points are uniformly distributed inside a
       square, Bucketing took around five days to generate the spanner. So, they engineered a
       practical parallel algorithm Fast-Sparse-Spanner, that generated geometric graphs fast
       and had average degrees close to those of greedy spanners. Fast-Sparse-Spanner could
       generate a 1.1-spanner for the same above point set in just 55 minutes, making it much faster
       than Bucketing in practice. They experimentally observed that Fast-Sparse-Spanner
       consistently generated t-spanners across a wide variety of distributions and real-world point
       sets. To check for the t-spanner property, they also devised an auxiliary practical stretch factor
       measurement algorithm, named Fast-Stretch-Factor, since Fast-Sparse-Spanner is
       not theoretically guaranteed to generate t-spanners. However, the weights and degrees of
       the generated graphs are far from the actual greedy spanners owing to the presence of long
       WSPD spanner edges, which form a backbone of their spanners. Despite the average degree
       of the generated graphs being close to those generated by Bucketing (see Table 1), the
       degrees and lightness values substantially differed. For the point set used in Table 1, the
       degrees of graphs generated by Fast-Sparse-Spanner and Bucketing were 78 and 18,
       respectively, and the lightness values were 16.7196 and 11.0354, respectively.
           Despite the progress made by Shariful et al. in [32], practical construction of spanners
       which closely resemble greedy spanners in terms of average degree, weight, and degree,
       especially for low t-values (≤ 2), remains an open problem. Note that Delaunay triangulations
       are 1.998-spanners [35] with O(n) edges that can be constructed in O(n log n) time (in practice,
       takes a few seconds even for millions of points). So, constructing t-spanners with t around 2
       or more is not considered challenging in practice.

       What are doppelgängers of greedy spanners? We introduce the notion of (a, b)-
       doppelgänger. A t-spanner H on a point set P is a (a, b)-doppelgänger of the greedy spanner
       G on P , if its average degree and lightness do not exceed those of G by more than additive
       constants a and b, respectively. Average degree and lightness are two central measures of
       spanner quality, and spanners with similar values for these metrics tend to be structurally
       similar. Thus, smaller values of a and b indicate better doppelgängers. Such doppelgängers
       are especially appealing to practitioners when they can be constructed significantly faster
       than the greedy spanner itself. The term “approximation” has not been used in this work
       intentionally, as the Approximate-Greedy [19] algorithm claims to generate spanners that
       are approximations of greedy spanners, but, in reality, they are structurally very different
       from the actual greedy spanners (also, see Table 1).

       Our contribution. Motivated by the lack of fast practical algorithm to generate (a, b)-
       doppelgängers of greedy spanners for low values of a and b, we design and engineer Θ-Greedy,
       a new spanner construction algorithm, based on Θ-Graph. We found Θ-Greedy to be
       considerably faster than our closest competitor Bucketing, and always produced high quality
       doppelgängers in our experiments. In our experiments, both a and b never exceeded 0.1. To
       our knowledge, no other known algorithm can achieve this while being fast and scalable in
       practice. See Figure 2 for a visual comparison between Θ-Greedy and Bucketing.

    We use the Θ-Graph as a seed spanner since it can be constructed fast in O(n log n)
time and, as seen in Table 1, excluding Fast-Sparse-Spanner (not guaranteed to produce
t-spanners), Θ-Graphs have the lowest average degree and thus the lowest number of edges.
We consider its edges by length and place them greedily, akin to Path-Greedy. Finally, we
find point pairs that do not have t-paths between them using a quad tree-based approach.
For every such point pair, we establish a t-path by placing edges carefully. Our algorithm
can leverage multiple cores for speedup.
    Θ-Greedy is designed as an engineering solution to a long-standing practical bottleneck
in geometric spanner construction rather than as a theoretical breakthrough. While its worst-
case complexity is O(n3 log n), the algorithm consistently exhibits near-quadratic scaling
in practice and uses linear space, enabling it to handle million-point datasets efficiently.
It leverages heuristic path checks and shortcut caching to achieve massive speedups, up
to ≈ 147x faster than Bucketing, while producing spanners that are structurally almost
indistinguishable from true greedy spanners in terms of degree and lightness. The focus of
Θ-Greedy is on simplicity, scalability, and reproducibility for real-world geometric networks,
not on improving asymptotic bounds.

        2     Description of Θ-Greedy
       This section presents the steps of the Θ-Greedy algorithm in order. Let H denote the
       output spanner constructed on the input point set P of size n. Initially, H is an empty graph.


       Step 1. Construct a minimum spanning tree M on P by running Prim’s algorithm on
       the edges of a Delaunay triangulation of P . Place the n − 1 edges of M in H. Since the
       Path-Greedy algorithm will place such edges, irrespective of the value of t, we can compute
       such edges quickly and place them in advance to avoid shortest-path calls.
       Step 2. Refer to Algorithm 1. We construct a Θ-Graph t-spanner GΘ on P . Let EΘ be
       the set of edges in GΘ . Sort the edges in EΘ in non-decreasing order of length. Then,
       process them greedily, following the spirit of the Path-Greedy algorithm: For each edge
       e = {u, v} ∈ EΘ , if no t-path exists between u and v in H, insert {u, v} into H; otherwise,
       skip the edge.
           To check for an t-path between u, v, we first invoke an heuristic algorithm called Greedy-
       Path, which avoids the use of a priority queue, unlike standard shortest-path algorithms such
       as A∗ or Dijkstra. This heuristic is inspired by the work [32]. We make use of shortcuts,
       as described next, to speed it up. The Greedy-Path performs a walk from u to v in H,
       aiming to discover a path greedily, whose total length does not exceed t · |uv|. At each step,
       it evaluates candidate next hops drawn from two sources: (i) precomputed t-paths obtained
       by previous Greedy-Path and A∗ calls, stored in shortcuts, as described next (also see
       Algorithm 1), and (ii) the actual graph neighbors of the current vertex. For every candidate,
       it computes a simple score - the current path length greedily constructed so far plus the
       edge (or shortcut) cost to that candidate, plus its straight-line (Euclidean) distance to v as
       an optimistic estimate of continuing via that vertex. It then moves to the candidate with
       the lowest score, marking visited choices to avoid cycling, and it stops immediately if v is
       reached. If the accumulated path length exceeds the stretch upper bound, the heuristic
       declares failure; otherwise, it returns the achieved t-path.
           If Greedy-Path finds a t-path, we store it as a shortcut (with its weight) in a structure
       shortcuts, similar to an adjacency list, to accelerate future queries. If Greedy-Path fails,
       we fall back to the popular A∗ algorithm. If A∗ also fails, we insert u, v into H; otherwise,
       we store the discovered t-path in shortcuts for future use. Note that to maintain the linear
       size of shortcuts, it is not updated in Steps 3, 4, and 5 of our algorithm.
       Step 3. Construct a region quad tree T on P such that the number of points contained inside
       every leaf is no more than a fixed constant ℓ. In our experiments, we found that ℓ = 1000
       was sufficient. For every leaf σ ∈ T , ensure that a t-path exists in Hσ , between all point
       pairs in σ, where Hσ is a subgraph of H, induced by the points in σ. This is achieved by
       running Dijkstra from every point in σ. Let S be the set of point pairs from all the leaves
       that do not have t-paths in H. Sort S, and place edges greedily. Akin to Step 2, we first use
       Greedy-Path, followed by A∗ , if necessary. While adding edges greedily, we check for the
       existence of t-paths by considering H rather than Hσ .
       Step 4. Let E ′ be an empty set of edges. For every leaf pair σi , σj ∈ T , ensure t-paths in H
       between all point pairs u ∈ σi , v ∈ σj . If a pair {u, v} is found not to have a t-path in H, place
       the edge {u, v} in H and add the same to E ′ . Akin to Step 2, we use Greedy-Path followed
       by A∗ . For a given leaf pair σi , σj , the t-paths (bridges connecting distant point pairs) found
       are temporarily stored in a list B. Since |σi | · |σj | ≤ ℓ2 = O(1), |B| = O(1). Its use is based
       on the observation that points from faraway tend to share t-paths. Consequently, we save

   Next, we show in Theorem 1 that H is a sparse t-spanner on P .

▶ Theorem 1. For any fixed t > 1, H is a t-spanner with O(n) edges.

Proof. The algorithm begins by inserting the edges of a minimum spanning tree M into H.
Since M is connected and contains exactly n − 1 edges, H is connected after Step 1. In Step
2, we place O(n) edges since the size of GΘ is O(n), for fixed t. Step 3 introduces O(n) edges
as ℓ is a constant. We insert at most 2ℓ = O(1) edges within each leaf of T , and since T has
O(n) leaves, the total number of edges added is O(n). If Step 4 places at most n edges, then
clearly, H has O(n) edges.
    Now, let us assume that the number of edges placed in Step 4 exceeds n (possibly ω(n)).
In what follows, we argue that in such a scenario, Step 5 places O(n) edges, thereby proving
our sparsity claim for H.
    Let u be any vertex of H. We claim that the number of edges placed in Step 5, that
are incident on u, is at most ⌈2π/α⌉, such that α satisfies the inequality, cos α + t sin α ≤ t.
Assume, for contradiction, that two edges {u, v} and {u, w} are added in Step 5, where
|uv| ≤ |uw|, and both lie in the same cone (with angle θ ≤ α). Since the edge {u, v} was
processed first, it is already in the graph when {u, w} is considered. For the edge {u, w} to
be prevented from insertion into H, the path Pu,w going through v must provide a t-path in
H: |Pu,w | ≤ t · |uw|.
    We analyze the worst-case geometric configuration where v and w are located on the two
distinct bounding rays of the cone, maximizing the distance |vw| for angle α. Refer to Figure 3.
An upper bound on |Pu,w | can be given by the distance projected onto the ray containing v plus

       Time complexity. Step 1 runs in O(n log n) time as Delaunay triangulations can be con-
       structed in O(n log n) time (via Voronoi diagram) having at most 3n edges and Prim’s
       algorithm on O(n) edges runs to completion in O(n log n) time. Next, the construction of
       the Θ-Graph GΘ takes O(n log n) time [28]. Also, |EΘ | = O(n). For every pair {u, v} ∈ EΘ ,
       verifying the existence of a t-path between u, v takes O(n) + O(n log n) = O(n log n) time
       in the worst-case due to the use of Greedy-Path that runs in O(n) time followed by A∗
       that runs in O(n log n) time in the worst-case. For O(n) pairs in EΘ , the total time taken
       is O(n2 log n). So, Step 2 runs in O(n2 log n) time. In Step 3, constructing T takes O(n2 )
       time in the worst case. The remaining part of this step takes O(n) time since the size of
       every leaf is at most ℓ = O(1). For every leaf of T , there are O(1) point pairs not having
       t-paths. For O(n) leaves, there are O(n) such point pairs. Detecting such pairs takes O(n)
       time since the size of every Hσ is O(1). Finally, Steps 4 and 5 each take O(n3 log n) time
       since there are O(n2 ) non-empty leaf pairs of T and for every such pair we spend O(n log n)
       time for detecting t-paths between ≤ ℓ2 = O(1) point pairs. Thus, the overall worst-case
       time complexity of Θ-Greedy is O(n3 log n).


       Remark on high time complexity. Although Θ-Greedy has a worst-case complexity of
       O(n3 log n), this bound is highly pessimistic. It assumes that Steps 4 and 5 spend O(n log n)
       time for every leaf-pair due to A∗ calls. In practice, this scenario rarely occurs. First, A∗
       is seldom invoked because Greedy-Path successfully finds t-paths in most cases. When
       Greedy-Path is used, its directional exploration visits only a small fraction of vertices before
       terminating, making each check extremely fast. Second, when a long t-path is discovered
       between two distant leaves σi , σj , it typically suffices for almost all point pairs p ∈ σi , q ∈ σj ,
       greatly reducing the number of subsequent calls. Combined with bridge reuse and shortcut
       caching, these effects make Steps 4 and 5 far cheaper than the worst-case analysis suggests.
       As a result, Θ-Greedy exhibits near-quadratic scaling in practice, as confirmed by our
       experiments on diverse synthetic and real-world datasets in Section 3.

Space complexity. The extra space needed by Prim’s algorithm and the Delaunay trian-
gulation construction in Step 1 is O(n). Constructing and storing GΘ takes O(n) space.
Greedy-Path and A∗ takes O(n) extra space. The data structure shortcuts uses O(n)
space since, in the worst case, it can contain one t-path per edge in GΘ . The quad tree T in
Step 4 uses O(dn) space, where d is its height. So, the extra space required by Θ-Greedy is
O(dn + |E ′ |) = O(dn), since |E ′ | ≤ n. Thus, Θ-Greedy behaves like a linear-space algorithm
in practice, making it possible to generate spanners on point sets where n is as large as 106 .

 3      Experiments
Setup. The algorithms were implemented in C++23 using GCC 13 and the CGAL 6.1 lib-
rary [33]. The boost library was used for common algorithms and data structures. Refer
to Table 2. All experiments were conducted on a desktop running Ubuntu Linux 24.04
LTS, equipped with an Intel Core i9-12900K processor and 32 GB of RAM. From CGAL,

Synthetic point set distributions. We used five point set distributions to generate random
point sets. These distributions were adopted from previous experimental studies [6, 9, 23, 29,
32]. They are named uni-square, normal-clustered, grid-random, annulus, and spokes.
Refer to Figure 4 for an illustration.
    The uni-square distribution generates points uniformly within a square region using
CGAL::Random_points_in_square_2. It is the most common distribution used in geometry
experiments. The normal-clustered distribution places points in randomly positioned
clusters, where each cluster follows a normal distribution with a fixed mean and standard
deviation. Since the clusters are separated by long distances, shortest-path calls tend to take
a long time. Hence, we chose it for our experiments. The grid-random distribution scatters
points across a non-contiguous grid within a scaled square, with integer coordinates chosen
uniformly at random. This distribution is important because of the collinearity present
throughout its point sets. In Figure 4, although it resembles uni-square, the coordinates
of the points are restricted to integers. The annulus distribution positions points inside
a ring-shaped region defined by inner and outer radii, using real-valued uniform sampling.
This distribution is important because of the large hole present inside the point sets. The
spokes distribution organizes points along five radial spokes emanating from a central point.
The vast separation between the collinear spokes is useful for testing spanner algorithms.
For each of the above distributions, we considered eight values of n, selected from the
set {1K, 2K, . . . , 128K}. For every value of n, we sampled five point sets.

        uniform patterns, which may significantly influence spanner construction time and structural

 4     Conclusions

We introduced Θ-Greedy, a practical parallel algorithm for constructing doppelgängers
of greedy geometric spanners that are structurally and metrically almost indistinguishable
from the actual greedy spanners. Thus, Θ-Greedy spanners serve as practical and reliable
alternatives to true greedy spanners. In our experiments, we found that Θ-Greedy con-
sistently achieved almost-greedy sparsity, lightness, and degree distribution while scaling
to million-point instances with linear space and significant speedups over Bucketing, the
fastest known greedy spanner algorithm. Our results close a long-standing gap between theor-
etical optimality and practical feasibility for low stretch factors, offering the first engineered
solution that combines simplicity, efficiency, accuracy, and scalability for large real-world
geometric networks.
    An exciting avenue for future work is reducing the worst-case time complexity of Θ-
Greedy without sacrificing its ability to produce doppelgängers. Exploring distribution-
sensitive optimizations and GPU acceleration could further broaden its applicability. Addi-
tionally, extending these ideas to higher dimensions remains a compelling open problem.
